977b83a1eb23: The trade’s handbook gave Thomas Nielsen Silkjær half a column: born, father, married, school, vessel, address. The court entered him in six registers, and the prison in four.
f1f5f197f197: The case can be followed day by day: from journal number 48 in the district bailiff’s police journal, through the six court days of the examinations in the court books, to the judgment in the register of judgments and prisoner no. 240 at Vridsløselille. In August 2026 the criminal file itself was added — the folder from Ringkøbing with the prosecutor’s and the defence counsel’s pleadings and the series of exhibits A—K, from the constable’s report to the telegram about the arrest. The chronicle tells the case in the registers’ own words — even where they are hard to bear. The most important entries are given in transcription at the end of the chapter. [S176]
24480ea3c5b7: Ten years after the wreck Kristiane married again — the fisherman <t1>Thomas Nielsen Silkjær</t1>, almost nine years her junior. But the story begins two years before the wedding. On 4 May 1904 she gave birth to a son, <t2>Kristen Lauridsen Silkjær</t2>, at Årgab. She was a widow of thirty-one; the parish register recorded Thomas Nielsen Silkjær as the named father. So the boy bore his father’s byname from birth. [S70]
ea3f63312012: The godparents at the baptism all came from Kristiane’s own world on the dunes: her father, the farmer Simon Enevoldsen of Haurvig, the girl Sidsel Enevoldsen, the fisheries inspector <t1>Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen</t1> of Bjerregaard and the bachelor Niels Christian Jespersen of Årgab. It was her parish, and they were her people — godparents were taken from the parish’s own circle, and Husby lay a day’s journey away. Then notice the fisheries inspector: Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen was the father of her drowned first husband. He stood godfather to the child, was a witness at her new marriage two years later, appeared in court in 1913 as Kristine Oline’s guardian and the same year again stood godfather in the family (chapter 13). Four times in nine years, across a child born outside marriage, a new marriage and a criminal case: her former in-laws did not turn their backs on her. [S70, S71, S120]
385b32528dc1: Thomas was then a young fisherman from Husby. The levying roll follows him: he stood without a break in the Husby levy district until 1906 and fished — as the prison register later summed it up — partly at Esbjerg, partly at Ringkøbing. The census of 1 February 1901 finds the nineteen-year-old as a farmhand with Peder Sand Pedersen on cadastral no. 67 in Klit By in Vedersø parish — the enumerator wrote him down as “Tomas Nielsen Silkær”, unmarried, born on 10 January 1882 in Husby. In September 1903 he was given a seaman’s book and went to sea, and at the draft board he was called up for the Navy, where he did his national service from September 1905 to April 1906. So both registers recorded the son with the farm name — the roll as <t1>Silkjær</t1>, the census as <t2>Silkær</t2> — while the roll at the same time records the father patronymically as <t3>Thomsen</t3>. The state’s own registers used the byname years before the name certificate. [S72, S74]
d68187ec3256: Twelve days after his discharge, on 5 May 1906, they were married in Haurvig Church. She stood as a widow at Årgab, he as a bachelor in Esbjerg; the witnesses were her father and her former father-in-law. A week later he was given a removal certificate, and on 21 May he registered in the Esbjerg levy district. Four weeks from man-of-war to husband with an address in the town. [S71, S72]
e791a59585fc: He came into the house as stepfather to three: Enevold Jepsen, b. 1892, Simon, b. 1894, and <t1>Kristine Oline</t1>, b. 1896. She was nine — twelve days from turning ten.
19988fb08ff5: The couple settled first in Esbjerg — their daughter Anna was born there in 1907 — and then came to Årgab, where they took over her in-laws’ property. He himself put a date on it in court: settled residence at Årgab <t1>from 1 April 1908</t1>. The levying roll only transfers him to the Holmsland Klit levy district in 1910, the same year their son Niels was born at Årgab — notices of removal often lagged behind the moves, and his own statement is the dated source for the takeover itself. [S72, S120]
e9287ab285af: The place was not large: room for four cows and two small horses, bought for 5,000 kroner and — in the register’s words — on condition of taking over a larger retirement settlement that rested on the property. It was mortgaged for the same amount as the purchase price; if it were sold, nothing would be left. On top of that a share in a motor boat, bought on a guaranteed loan and used for fishing and freight between Årgab and Ringkøbing, and a share in pound nets and gear that were wearing out. He put the income himself at 1,000—1,200 kroner a year. This is the house the rest of the chapter takes place in: a household with children of two marriages, debt on everything and one breadwinner. [S120]
4bd9568ada43: The collapse became visible before the case. The neighbour on the dunes was the smallholder <t1>Thyge Nielsen</t1>, and his daughter was called <t2>Nielsine Nielsen</t2> — born at Årgab on 23 November 1887, unmarried, twenty-five years old in the autumn of 1912. In late summer Kristiane had noticed that her husband often called at Thyge Nielsen’s, and there was talk in the district. She asked him straight out whether there was anything between him and the daughter; he firmly denied it, and she believed him. There <t3>was</t3> something: he later admitted in court that he and Nielsine had already had intercourse several times by then — in her room at her parents’, while the families lived as neighbours. [S120, S130]
b7737b792ce6: On 14 December 1912 he left home in secret together with her. They went first to <t1>Kiel</t1>, where he looked for work but was expelled before he found any, and then to <t2>Copenhagen</t2>, where they lived together — the register’s words are <t3>“as man and wife”</t3>. In court he later declared that it had been his intention <t4>not</t4> to return to his wife or his home. [S120]
c189c381232a: The police report in the criminal file tells what the registers do not: the families searched themselves before the police did. Nielsine’s father, Thyge Nielsen, went after the couple and found them <t1>between Christmas and New Year in Kiel</t1>, where Thomas had taken lodgings as <t2>“fisherman Thomas Nielsen and wife from Esbjerg”</t2>. When it came out that this was not true, the police expelled him, and they both went back with the father to Vamdrup — but there they left him and bought tickets, apparently to Fredericia. From there they went on to Copenhagen. The closest anyone from home later came to them was a chance in the dark: a marine from Bjerregaard — the report records him as Otto Hejde — saw them one evening around New Year pass by in the street while he was standing guard at <t3>the Yellow Palace</t3>. Seen and gone again; where they were living, no one at home knew. [S176]
e072fa32973e: Back at Årgab Kristiane was left with the children, the debt — and a stepdaughter carrying something no one in the house had yet put into words.
a34ab2f99890: Kristine Oline was sixteen, pregnant and alone with it. The man who had made her pregnant was her stepfather, and he had gone. Her mother knew nothing. The adult outside the house she chose to confide in was not from the dunes.
e7d351f54d2c: <t1>Pastor Hornbech</t1> of Randers was an itinerant preacher and had in recent years visited the dunes several times — and had talked with her along the way. Behind the register’s name stands in all probability <t2>Carl Marius Hornbech</t2>: a pastor’s son, a graduate of Randers grammar school, a missionary in India from 1902 until his wife died out there in 1908 — the year after, he came home as an itinerant preacher and lived in Randers in exactly the years the register speaks of. The police report in the criminal file records him precisely as <t3>“itinerant preacher for the Danish Missionary Society”</t3> — the society Hornbech travelled for. A man who had himself known loss. The church mission milieu that the revival on the dunes had made part of her world reached far beyond the parish. Through it she had met him; now that connection became her way out. Without her mother’s knowledge she wrote to the pastor in Randers and confided in him — about the pregnancy, and about who the father was.
2192c435b99c: Hornbech answered with a letter in which he charged her to confide in her mother. How it then came about, Kristiane herself told in court on 7 March, and the register has preserved the scene: the daughter handed her the pastor’s letter and left the room. The mother read it and went in to her. The police report in the criminal file puts a date on the evening: <t1>Thursday 13 February 1913</t1>. [S176]
3d26fc14a119: …after the deponent had read the letter, she went in to her daughter, who thereupon, <t1>with strong emotion and in tears</t1>, confirmed to the deponent what she had told the pastor, and on the deponent’s express question firmly declared that she had had nothing to do with other men and that the prisoner was therefore the father of the expected child.
8c6b2a11b029: Police register p. 153 · Kristiane’s statement, 7 March 1913 · deponent (Cpd.) = Kristiane, prisoner (Arr.) = the accused [S120]
222f8b59c8ed: That is how the case came to light: not by a report from neighbours, not by a midwife or a doctor — but because a sixteen-year-old girl wrote a letter to a pastor, and the pastor answered her seriously and pointed her home to her mother. The mission milieu’s network had given her an adult outside the house to write to.
e625de491625: Hornbech’s letter itself has not been found — not among the exhibits of the criminal file either — but report A independently confirms that the pastor had <t1>“received letters from the girl made pregnant about the matter”</t1>; on the letter and on the identification of the pastor, see caveat 35. The scene stands as Kristiane told it in court, reported by the clerk of the court. [S120, S174, S176]

95d0183c315e: The birth of the case itself can now be followed to the day — it is in the constable’s report, exhibit A of the case. <t1>On the evening of Thursday 13 February</t1> Anders Hejde came home to Bjerregaard from Randers. There he had met Pastor Hornbech, and the pastor had told him what he knew from the letters: that Thomas Silkjær’s stepdaughter was pregnant, and by whom. Hejde took the message to Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen — Kristine Oline’s paternal grandfather, who was staying in Bjerregaard just then. That same Thursday evening, in the house at Årgab, Kristine Oline handed her mother the pastor’s letter. The next morning the grandfather travelled to Årgab <t2>“to have the matter looked into more closely”</t2> — <t3>“but Christine had by then already confided in her mother”</t3>. What had been hidden since the summer of 1911 became shared knowledge in a single evening. [S176]
a807d8b10e28: On Monday 17 February Constable Jensen was at Årgab. His report opens in the formulaic language of the time — and with one fact the registers do not have: <t1>“… and the proper persons concerned have moreover wished the matter to be made the subject of public investigation”</t1>. The family itself asked for the investigation. Four statements were taken that same day — the grandfather, Kristiane, Kristine Oline herself and Thyge Nielsen — and, for use in the search, a description of the man who had left: <t2>“a little under middle height … very fair moustache; he is ruddy and speaks West Jutland dialect”</t2>. [S176]

a42ca6c3a214: The same day the district bailiff’s office gave the case journal number 48. In the journal’s column for the nature of the case the clerk wrote: <t1>“Breach of Penal Code § 162 (impregnation of stepdaughter)”</t1>. From there every step can be followed in the journal’s column of dispatches: the next day a letter went to the Copenhagen police, and on 21 February the answer came by telegram — <t2>arrested</t2>. [S124]
5dabd7c8ea66: The letter of 18 February lies in the file as exhibit B. The bailiff asked the Copenhagen police to search for the accused, <t1>“if need be circulated in P. E.”</t1> — Politiets Efterretninger, the police’s own nationwide gazette — and if found, to arrest him, question him and telegraph. The bailiff wrote why: [S176]

9c64082d2fbf: The arrest itself is in exhibit C of the case, the extract from the register of the Copenhagen Criminal and Police Court. <t1>On Friday 21 February at a quarter to seven in the morning</t1> he was found on the corner of Strandgade and Torvegade in Christianshavn and taken to the police station. At 8 o’clock he was handed over to the Nytorv jail, and at half past eleven — barely five hours after the arrest — he had been brought before the Criminal and Police Court as examination no. 575. He confessed at once: he had had intercourse with his stepdaughter many times, and <t2>“he dare not deny that he has made his stepdaughter pregnant”</t2>. The court closed the case <t3>“for transcription, to be sent together with the arrested man to the bailiff in Ringkjøbing”</t3> — the man and the papers were to go the same way. The same day the telegram arrived in Ringkøbing, written in pencil on the state telegraph’s form, exhibit D of the case: <t4>“Thommas Nielsen Silkjør found brought before court arrested to be collected here.”</t4> [S176]

fec6ea539c99: And then it became public. <t1>Politiets Efterretninger</t1> — the gazette the bailiff’s letter had pointed to — carried him the day after the arrest, in no. 23 of 22 February, under the heading <t2>“Arrested for crimes etc.”</t2>; three days later, in no. 24 of 25 February, he stood again under <t3>“Handed over to other jurisdictions”</t3> with the addition <t4>“To Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds”</t4> — the transfer to the jail in Ringkøbing, set in print. Two lines in a gazette that went out to every police station in the country: the case from the dunes was no longer anybody’s secret. [S177]
46e4eb0e5958: On 24 February at half past eleven he was brought before the police court at the court house — in the absence of the regular judge the examination was conducted by the acting deputy <t1>H. Gronenberg</t1>. He repeated his confession, and the judge decreed custody. Here the register has a note that was later struck out: under D a service book (skudsmålsbog) for Kristine Oline was filed — the entry is struck through with wavy lines. In the preserved criminal file, however, D is the telegram about the arrest; so the service book did not go into the final series of exhibits, and the letter was reused. The case was given the police court number 26/13, and the list of cases then records six court days: 24 and 28 February, 7, 17, 22 and 26 March. [S120, S121, S176]
bcbda3a9d5d4: On 28 February — now before deputy <t1>Th. Edsberg</t1>, in the judge’s absence through illness — he gave his detailed statement. The marriage had by his account been very happy until last summer, when the connection with Nielsine began. About his stepdaughter he admitted everything: intercourse many times since the summer of 1911 — the first time one evening at harvest time, in the barn of the property at Årgab. She was fifteen, just turned. He maintained that she had never been forced — and in the same statement admitted something that turns his own claim around: [S120]
